verdict.reasoning: Patient reports wheeze starting about two days ago and associated shortness of breath: "it started, like, about two days ago" and "I'm feeling like a little bit, uh, uh, short of breath."

Symptoms began after house-cleaning with dust and came on over about an hour: "I was, like, cleaning the house. And, like, um, all this dust came out of the, the carpet" and when asked if it started suddenly or gradually: "it started after maybe, uh, an hour or so."
Patient states symptoms are worse at night and affect her ability to complete sentences: "it get's a bit worse, um, at night" and "sometimes, um, I'm unable to , complete my sentences."
Patient denies pain with deep breaths and denies dizziness: "Mmm, no, no. No pain." and "Uh, no. No dizziness. Uh, none of that."
Fluid intake is reported as "four or five glasses a day": "Yeah, yeah. I think I'm having, like, you know, four or five glasses a day."

She reports childhood asthma with exertional symptoms and seasonal hay fever: "I used to have, like, a bit of, um, asthma, uh, as a child"; "sometimes when I, um, run for, like, long periods, it can, it can start up a bit"; and "also in the summer I sometimes get, um, hay fever."

Transcript notes she has an inhaler from a couple of months ago but does not say she has not used it for months or that it is specifically a SABA: "I have, uh, I have, like, an asthma inhaler. I use that" and "I think I might have one from, like, a couple of months ago." The claimed non-use for months and SABA type are not stated and conflict with "I use that."

Doctor asks: "apart from this, do you know if you're allergic to anything?" and patient replies: "Uh, not that I know of." This supports "no known allergies" generally, but earlier she suspects dust allergy and has known hay fever. Stating simply "no known allergies" without context of these is an oversimplifying new assertion.

Doctor explicitly suspects asthma or allergy related to dust: "given you've got a history of asthma and hay fever. This could be one of two things. But, we want to rule out asthma or an allergy first" and advises antihistamine "in case it is an allergy you've had from the dust."

Transcript indicates past asthma with occasional symptoms on long runs and intermittent inhaler use, but does not characterize current control as "sub-optimally controlled": "did it resolve when you were a child?" ... "I think mostly, yeah... sometimes when I, um, run for, like, long periods, it can, it can start up a bit. But, um, I have, uh, I have, like, an asthma inhaler." No explicit assessment of current control is given.

Doctor plans in-person GP review with pulse oximetry: "what you'll need is visit one of our clinics, so we can do some more tests" and "use a small device on your finger, to check the amount of oxygen in your blood." Timing is effectively same-day given the immediate referral context.
The transcript only mentions pulse oximetry: "use a small device on your finger, to check the amount of oxygen in your blood." Spirometry and peak-flow are not mentioned.

Doctor advises OTC antihistamine, possibly obtained on the way: "if you've got something, like an antihistamine, which you normally take for hay fever at home, I would take one" and when she has none: "You might be able to get one on your way to the doctor's surgery. If not, they can prescribe you one."

Doctor notes possible need for steroids pending assessment: "you may need to take some steroids now. But, we cannot... know until we've done those tests first." This implies the GP will decide on steroids or other therapy after assessment.
Doctor states they will send a letter to the GP via the app: "I'm gonna write a letter for your GP, just to let him know what's happened" and "you should get the letter over the app."
